en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Rattandhakāravagga 14.
The Second Training Rule on Exhortation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was standing alone with a man on a carriage road, in a cul-de-sac, and at a crossroads;
she conversed with him, whispered into his ear, and even sent away her companion bhikkhunī.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [as before]... were indignant, complained, and spread it about, saying:

“How indeed can the noble lady Thullanandā stand together with a man, converse with him, whisper into his ear, or send away a companion nun, even on a carriage road, in a cul-de-sac, or at a crossroads? … [The Buddha said:
“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā does so on a carriage road, in a cul-de-sac, or at a crossroads?”
“Does she stand together with one [nun], converse with her, whisper into her ear, and even dismiss a second nun?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her...
“How indeed, monks, could the bhikkhunī Thullanandā stand together with a man alone in a carriage road,
at a crossroads, or at a junction; how could she converse with him, whisper into his ear,
and even dismiss a companion bhikkhunī?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule:
‘If any bhikkhunī should stand alone with a man on a carriage road, in a cul-de-sac, or at a crossroads.’”
“Should she converse with her, or whisper into her ear, or send away a companion nun, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whoever” means whichever person... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the type of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"A carriage road" means:
"Street" is what is meant.
"Array" (byūha) means that they exit by the very same way they enter.
A "siṅghāṭaka" is called a crossroads.
A "man" is called...
A human being, not a *yakkha*, not a *peta*, and not an animal, is wise and capable of standing together and conversing.
"Together" (*saddhiṃ*) means on one side.
"By one person" means both a man and a nun.
"Should stand together" means...
If she stands within arm’s reach of a man, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Should converse" means:
if she converses while standing within arm’s reach of a man, there is an offense of expiation.
"Or she should whisper in the ear":
if she speaks into a man's ear, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Or she should send away a second nun": [if she does so, there is an offense of expiation].
If she wishes to practice improper conduct and dismisses even a second nun, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For her who leaves the range of sight or the range of hearing, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Once she has left [the range], there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If, having moved beyond arm’s reach, one stands together with or converses with [another], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one stands together with or converses with a yakkha, a peta, a paṇḍaka, or a human in animal form, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
If there is any wise person as a companion, one who is expectant of arahantship and intent on final knowledge,
whether standing or conversing, [one should speak].
Not wishing to engage in improper conduct,
she urges a second bhikkhunī to act when there is business to be done;
[this is not an offense] for one who is insane.
"For one who is a first offender.
The fourth training rule is concluded.
